extracted_claims.text: Article 43 of the EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689) sets out conformity assessment procedures for high-risk AI systems, giving providers two routes: internal control (Annex VI) or quality management system plus technical documentation assessment by a notified body (Annex VII).

For high-risk AI systems listed in point 1 of Annex III (biometrics), the provider may choose internal control or notified-body assessment depending on whether harmonised standards/common specifications have been applied.

Annex VII (notified body) assessment is mandatory for certain systems, such as biometric identification and systems under Annex I product-safety legislation / critical infrastructure, while most other high-risk AI systems may use the self-assessment Annex VI route.

For high-risk AI systems already covered by existing EU product legislation listed in Annex I, Section A, providers must follow the conformity assessment procedures of that existing legislation, with notified bodies also verifying compliance with the AI-specific requirements.

Providers may choose any notified body for the Annex VII procedure, except that where a high-risk AI system is to be put into service by law enforcement, immigration or asylum authorities or EU institutions/bodies/offices/agencies, the relevant market surveillance authority acts as the notified body.
Substantial modifications to a high-risk AI system require a new conformity assessment, except for predetermined changes in systems that continue to learn after being placed on the market.

Article 46 allows a market surveillance authority, by way of derogation from Article 43 and upon a duly justified request, to authorise the placing on the market or putting into service of specific high-risk AI systems for a limited period for exceptional reasons of public security, protection of life/health, environmental protection, or protection of key industrial/infrastructural assets.

Under Annex VII, where necessary and after other reasonable means to verify conformity have been exhausted, a notified body may, upon reasoned request, be granted access to the training and trained models of the AI system, including relevant parameters, subject to IP and confidentiality protections.
Article 43(5) gives the European Commission power to adopt delegated acts under Article 97 to update Annex VI and Annex VII in light of technical progress.
Article 35 of the AI Act establishes rules on identification numbers and lists of notified bodies.

A Council document (7322/26) sets out a coding scheme (e.g., AIP 0101–0105) designating the scope of conformity assessment bodies notified under Article 30 for AI systems subject to Annex I categories.

A Commission/Council proposal (COM(2025) 836, document ST-15708-2025-INIT) proposes a new Annex XIV listing codes and categories of AI systems for the NANDO notified/designated organisations information system, and proposes amendments to Regulation (EU) 2018/1139 to integrate AI Act high-risk requirements, as well as entry-into-force rules.

As of March 2026, the notified body ecosystem for the AI Act is still being built, with designation processes ongoing across Member States, limited capacity, and uncertain timelines ahead of the August 2026 deadline.
As of April 2026, no notified bodies had been formally designated under the AI Act according to one industry blog tracking MDR/IVDR interplay.

One source states that post-2026, notified bodies designated under the AI Act will begin conducting AI Act-specific conformity assessments, with the intersection with MDR/IVDR notified body assessments continuing to develop; it also states August 2026 is the deadline for full application of high-risk AI obligations.
As of October 2025, the NANDO system listed 51 MDR-designated notified bodies and 19 IVDR-designated notified bodies (these are medical-device regulation designations, not AI Act designations).

NANDO (New Approach Notified and Designated Organisations) is the Commission's information system used to publish lists of designated notified bodies, filterable by legislation, including for medical devices.

For the Cyber Resilience Act (a separate but related EU regulation), as of late June 2026 zero notified bodies had been designated in NANDO, with a target of 11 December 2026 for sufficient notified body capacity and full application from 11 December 2027.

report:
# Conformity Assessment Procedures for High-Risk AI Systems Under the EU AI Act

## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689) establishes two main routes for conformity assessment of high-risk AI systems—internal control or notified-body assessment—with the stricter route reserved for certain categories such as biometrics and systems already covered by product-safety legislation (high confidence). However, the notified-body ecosystem needed to operationalize third-party assessments appears substantially unbuilt as of early-to-mid 2026, and no source provides a confirmed, named list of bodies formally designated under the AI Act itself.

## Key Findings

### Conformity Assessment Procedures
Article 43 of the AI Act gives providers of high-risk AI systems two possible routes: internal control under Annex VI, or a combination of quality management system review plus technical documentation assessment by a notified body under Annex VII (low confidence) ([securiti.ai](https://securiti.ai/eu-ai-act/article-43), [dpo-consulting.com](https://www.dpo-consulting.com/blog/ai-conformity-assessment), [fpf.org](https://fpf.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/OT-comformity-assessment-under-the-eu-ai-act-WP-1.pdf)). For systems listed in Annex III, point 1 (biometrics), providers may choose between internal control or notified-body assessment depending on whether harmonised standards or common specifications have been applied (low confidence) ([futurium.ec.europa.eu](https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2021-10/Kop_EU%20Artificial%20Intelligence%20Act%20-%20The%20European%20Approach%20to%20AI_21092021_0.pdf)). Some industry commentary suggests Annex VII assessment is mandatory for biometric identification systems and those falling under critical infrastructure/product-safety legislation, while most other high-risk systems may rely on self-assessment (low confidence) ([quantamixsolutions.com](https://quantamixsolutions.com/insights/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment)).

For high-risk systems already regulated under existing EU product legislation (Annex I, Section A), providers must follow that legislation's conformity assessment procedures, with notified bodies additionally verifying AI-specific requirements (high confidence) ([ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43), [vde.com](https://www.vde.com/topics-en/artificial-intelligence/blog/conformity-assessment-high-risk-ai)). Providers may generally select any notified body for Annex VII assessments, except that for systems used by law enforcement, immigration, asylum authorities, or EU institutions, the relevant market surveillance authority performs this role (medium confidence) ([ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/ga/ai-act/article-43)). Substantial modifications generally trigger a new conformity assessment, with an exception for predetermined changes in continuously learning systems (medium confidence) ([ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43)). Article 46 permits market surveillance authorities to derogate from Article 43 and authorize temporary market placement for exceptional public-security, health, environmental, or infrastructure reasons (medium confidence) ([ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-46)). Under Annex VII, notified bodies may, as a last resort and subject to IP/confidentiality safeguards, request access to training and trained models (medium confidence) ([ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/annex-7)). Article 43(5) reportedly empowers the Commission to update Annexes VI and VII via delegated acts (low confidence) ([fpf.org](https://fpf.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/OT-comformity-assessment-under-the-eu-ai-act-WP-1.pdf)).

### Notified Body Designation & Infrastructure
Article 35 establishes rules for identification numbers and lists of notified bodies (low confidence) ([regulation-ai.eu](https://www.regulation-ai.eu/en/articles/article-35)). A Council document (ST-7322-2026-INIT) reportedly sets out a coding scheme (AIP 0101–0105) for designating conformity assessment bodies' scope under Article 30 (medium confidence) ([data.consilium.europa.eu](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-7322-2026-INIT/en/pdf)). A related Commission/Council proposal (COM(2025) 836) proposes a new Annex XIV for the NANDO system and amendments integrating AI Act requirements with aviation safety regulation (medium confidence) ([data.consilium.europa.eu](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-15708-2025-INIT/en/pdf)). As of October 2025, NANDO listed 51 MDR-designated and 19 IVDR-designated notified bodies, but these are medical-device designations, not AI Act designations (high confidence) ([eur-lex.europa.eu](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A52025SC1051)).

### Timeline and Readiness
Multiple low-confidence sources suggest the notified-body ecosystem for the AI Act remained unbuilt as of March–April 2026, with designation processes ongoing and limited capacity ahead of the August 2026 deadline ([eyreact.com](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act); [aiact-navigator.com](https://aiact-navigator.com/blog/eu-ai-act-medical-devices-mdr-ivdr-interplay-guide)). A comparable pattern appears in the related Cyber Resilience Act, where zero notified bodies had been designated as of late June 2026 (low confidence) ([cybercertlabs.com](https://www.cybercertlabs.com/case-studies/insights-cra-notified-bodies-2026)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
Sources disagree on the precise state of AI Act notified-body designation in 2026: one states flatly that zero designations existed as of April 2026, while another (March 2026) describes an unfinished but ambiguous process (low confidence claims, below 0.4) ([aiact-navigator.com](https://aiact-navigator.com/blog/eu-ai-act-medical-devices-mdr-ivdr-interplay-guide), [eyreact.com](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act)). An earlier 2022 proposal text of Article 43 predates the final Regulation 2024/1689 and should not be treated as current law ([artificial-intelligence-act.com](https://www.artificial-intelligence-act.com/Artificial_Intelligence_Act_Article_43_(Proposal_25.11.2022).html)).

## Knowledge Gaps
No source provides a confirmed, named list of bodies designated specifically under the AI Act as of October 2026. It remains unclear whether the Annex XIV/NANDO coding proposals have been formally adopted. The precise Annex III categories requiring mandatory notified-body assessment versus self-assessment are not comprehensively documented, nor are the enforcement consequences of apparent gaps in notified-body capacity ahead of the August 2026 deadline.

# Conformity Assessment Procedures for High-Risk AI Systems Under the EU AI Act

## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689) establishes two main routes for conformity assessment of high-risk AI systems—internal control or notified-body assessment—with the stricter route reserved for certain categories such as biometrics and systems already covered by product-safety legislation (high confidence). However, the notified-body ecosystem needed to operationalize third-party assessments appears substantially unbuilt as of early-to-mid 2026, and no source provides a confirmed, named list of bodies formally designated under the AI Act itself.

## Key Findings

### Conformity Assessment Procedures
Article 43 of the AI Act gives providers of high-risk AI systems two possible routes: internal control under Annex VI, or a combination of quality management system review plus technical documentation assessment by a notified body under Annex VII (low confidence) ([securiti.ai](https://securiti.ai/eu-ai-act/article-43), [dpo-consulting.com](https://www.dpo-consulting.com/blog/ai-conformity-assessment), [fpf.org](https://fpf.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/OT-comformity-assessment-under-the-eu-ai-act-WP-1.pdf)). For systems listed in Annex III, point 1 (biometrics), providers may choose between internal control or notified-body assessment depending on whether harmonised standards or common specifications have been applied (low confidence) ([futurium.ec.europa.eu](https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2021-10/Kop_EU%20Artificial%20Intelligence%20Act%20-%20The%20European%20Approach%20to%20AI_21092021_0.pdf)). Some industry commentary suggests Annex VII assessment is mandatory for biometric identification systems and those falling under critical infrastructure/product-safety legislation, while most other high-risk systems may rely on self-assessment (low confidence) ([quantamixsolutions.com](https://quantamixsolutions.com/insights/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment)).

For high-risk systems already regulated under existing EU product legislation (Annex I, Section A), providers must follow that legislation's conformity assessment procedures, with notified bodies additionally verifying AI-specific requirements (high confidence) ([ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43), [vde.com](https://www.vde.com/topics-en/artificial-intelligence/blog/conformity-assessment-high-risk-ai)). Providers may generally select any notified body for Annex VII assessments, except that for systems used by law enforcement, immigration, asylum authorities, or EU institutions, the relevant market surveillance authority performs this role (medium confidence) ([ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/ga/ai-act/article-43)). Substantial modifications generally trigger a new conformity assessment, with an exception for predetermined changes in continuously learning systems (medium confidence) ([ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43)). Article 46 permits market surveillance authorities to derogate from Article 43 and authorize temporary market placement for exceptional public-security, health, environmental, or infrastructure reasons (medium confidence) ([ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-46)). Under Annex VII, notified bodies may, as a last resort and subject to IP/confidentiality safeguards, request access to training and trained models (medium confidence) ([ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/annex-7)). Article 43(5) reportedly empowers the Commission to update Annexes VI and VII via delegated acts (low confidence) ([fpf.org](https://fpf.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/OT-comformity-assessment-under-the-eu-ai-act-WP-1.pdf)).

### Notified Body Designation & Infrastructure
Article 35 establishes rules for identification numbers and lists of notified bodies (low confidence) ([regulation-ai.eu](https://www.regulation-ai.eu/en/articles/article-35)). A Council document (ST-7322-2026-INIT) reportedly sets out a coding scheme (AIP 0101–0105) for designating conformity assessment bodies' scope under Article 30 (medium confidence) ([data.consilium.europa.eu](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-7322-2026-INIT/en/pdf)). A related Commission/Council proposal (COM(2025) 836) proposes a new Annex XIV for the NANDO system and amendments integrating AI Act requirements with aviation safety regulation (medium confidence) ([data.consilium.europa.eu](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-15708-2025-INIT/en/pdf)). As of October 2025, NANDO listed 51 MDR-designated and 19 IVDR-designated notified bodies, but these are medical-device designations, not AI Act designations (high confidence) ([eur-lex.europa.eu](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A52025SC1051)).

### Timeline and Readiness
Multiple low-confidence sources suggest the notified-body ecosystem for the AI Act remained unbuilt as of March–April 2026, with designation processes ongoing and limited capacity ahead of the August 2026 deadline ([eyreact.com](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act); [aiact-navigator.com](https://aiact-navigator.com/blog/eu-ai-act-medical-devices-mdr-ivdr-interplay-guide)). A comparable pattern appears in the related Cyber Resilience Act, where zero notified bodies had been designated as of late June 2026 (low confidence) ([cybercertlabs.com](https://www.cybercertlabs.com/case-studies/insights-cra-notified-bodies-2026)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
Sources disagree on the precise state of AI Act notified-body designation in 2026: one states flatly that zero designations existed as of April 2026, while another (March 2026) describes an unfinished but ambiguous process (low confidence claims, below 0.4) ([aiact-navigator.com](https://aiact-navigator.com/blog/eu-ai-act-medical-devices-mdr-ivdr-interplay-guide), [eyreact.com](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act)). An earlier 2022 proposal text of Article 43 predates the final Regulation 2024/1689 and should not be treated as current law ([artificial-intelligence-act.com](https://www.artificial-intelligence-act.com/Artificial_Intelligence_Act_Article_43_(Proposal_25.11.2022).html)).

## Knowledge Gaps
No source provides a confirmed, named list of bodies designated specifically under the AI Act as of October 2026. It remains unclear whether the Annex XIV/NANDO coding proposals have been formally adopted. The precise Annex III categories requiring mandatory notified-body assessment versus self-assessment are not comprehensively documented, nor are the enforcement consequences of apparent gaps in notified-body capacity ahead of the August 2026 deadline.
